Geophysics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 31k Articles: 835
Geophysics applies physics and mathematics to the structure, composition, and evolution of planets, including Earth. It connects measurements with mechanisms: plate tectonics explains moving crust, the geodynamo explains a planetary magnetic field, and albedo connects reflected sunlight to a planetary surface energy balance. Even a small model can reveal a useful organizing principle, such as the competition between ice-ocean albedo feedback and stabilizing thermal radiation.

Climatology

Climatological normal

Words: 34
Climatology OurBigBook.com
A climate statistic calculated over a stated long reference period, conventionally often 30 years. Specify the variable, site, period and averaging procedure; a changing climate makes the choice of baseline consequential.[ref]

Rock physics

Words: 43
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The study of how rock composition, structure, pressure, temperature, fluids and deformation determine measurable physical properties such as density, elastic wave speeds, electrical conductivity and attenuation. These relations are needed to interpret seismic tomography and gravity anomalies; one measured property rarely determines a unique material state.

Magnetic survey

Words: 69 Articles: 2
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Measurement of a magnetic field over a region to locate contrasts in subsurface magnetization. Temporal background changes and cultural interference must be distinguished from spatial magnetic anomalies.

Base-station magnetometer

Words: 23
Magnetic survey OurBigBook.com
A stationary magnetometer recording time variation of the background magnetic field while a moving instrument measures spatial variation. Subtracting the synchronized base changes reduces temporal contamination.

Proton-precession magnetometer (f=γp​∣B∣/(2π))

Words: 22
Magnetic survey OurBigBook.com
An absolute scalar magnetometer that infers ∣B∣ from the free Larmor precession frequency of polarized protons. It measures field strength rather than field direction.

Paleomagnetism

Words: 204 Articles: 4
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Study of ancient magnetic-field records preserved in rocks. Primary magnetizations can constrain former latitude and rotation, subject to age and alteration tests.

Remagnetization

Words: 40
Paleomagnetism OurBigBook.com
Acquisition of a younger remanent magnetization that partly or completely replaces an older magnetic record. Heating, chemical alteration or later mineral growth can cause it. A successful continental reconstruction must connect the age of the measured magnetic component to the geological event being reconstructed.

Paleomagnetic reversal test

Words: 40
Paleomagnetism OurBigBook.com
Test whether normal- and reversed-polarity remanent magnetization directions are statistically antipodal after suitable structural correction. Agreement supports recording of opposite polarities of the same large-scale magnetic field; failure can reveal overprints or other complications. Passing is not, by itself, proof of primary acquisition.

Paleomagnetic fold test

Words: 51
Paleomagnetism OurBigBook.com
Compare the scatter of remanent magnetization directions before and after correcting for folding. Improved agreement after restoring bedding supports acquisition before folding; agreement only in present coordinates supports a younger overprint. Partial unfolding can indicate acquisition during deformation or more complicated histories. The test constrains relative timing, rather than supplying an absolute age.

Apparent polar wander path

Words: 51
Paleomagnetism OurBigBook.com
A time-ordered sequence of ancient magnetic pole positions inferred from dated remanent magnetization in a continental block. The apparent motion includes the block's movement relative to the rotation axis and can include true polar wander. Consistent paths after a fixed relative rotation support an interval of shared motion; conventional paleomagnetism does not independently determine absolute longitude.

Geodynamic modelling

Words: 30
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Quantitative simulation of evolving planetary deformation, flow and thermal or compositional structure under specified physical laws and constitutive assumptions. Feasibility of a regime does not supply its historical onset date.

Air parcel

Words: 40
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
An air parcel is a small material volume followed through an atmospheric flow. The elementary parcel model assumes rapid pressure adjustment to its environment but negligible heat and material exchange during the displacement. Its potential temperature is conserved during reversible dry adiabatic process at fixed composition.

Regolith

Words: 23
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Loose fragmented material above coherent bedrock. On the Moon its fractures and debris strongly scatter seismic waves, complicating detection of weak deep-interior phases.

Geopotential (Φ)

Words: 71 Articles: 1
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The gravitational potential energy per unit mass, including the centrifugal contribution when using the effective gravity of a rotating planet. In a local atmosphere with approximately constant effective gravitational acceleration, Φ=gz up to a constant. Its horizontal gradient on an isobaric surface drives the balanced wind.

Geopotential surface (Φ=constant)

Words: 32
Geopotential OurBigBook.com
A surface on which geopotential is constant. Effective gravity is perpendicular to it. In a local constant-gravity approximation these surfaces are horizontal; comparing their slopes with isopycnals identifies the geometry permitting an adiabatic parcel exchange to release available potential energy.

Climate

Words: 76 Articles: 2
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The statistical properties of atmospheric and related oceanic conditions over an extended period, including means, variability and extremes. Radiation budgets, ocean circulation and atmospheric transport help determine its large-scale structure.

Paleoclimate

Words: 36
Climate OurBigBook.com
The climate of an earlier geological interval, inferred from dated geological, geochemical or biological indicators. Spatially coherent glacial deposits, striations and climate-sensitive rocks can test a continental reconstruction, provided their ages and original tectonic contexts are established.

Rain shadow

Words: 13
Climate OurBigBook.com
A region of reduced precipitation on the leeward side of a topographic barrier.

Radiation budget (R)

Words: 32
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The energy entering and leaving a system through electromagnetic radiation. A top-of-atmosphere radiation budget compares absorbed sunlight with outgoing thermal radiation. A latitude-dependent imbalance can be balanced by atmospheric and ocean heat fluxes even when the global mean is zero.

Geothermal gradient (dT/dz)

Words: 98 Articles: 1
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The geothermal gradient is the rate at which temperature varies with depth. For steady one-dimensional thermal conduction with constant thermal conductivity kT​, the magnitude of upward heat flux is q=kT​dT/dz.

Crustal mean temperature from conductive heat flow (Tc​=Ts​+qhc​/(2k))

Words: 75
Geothermal gradient OurBigBook.com
For a crustal layer of thickness hc​ with constant thermal conductivity k, no internal heating and a linear conductive profile, the upward heat flux magnitude q obeys Fourier's law, T(z)=Ts​+qz/k with depth positive downward. Depth averaging gives
Tc​=hc​1​∫0hc​​T(z)dz=Ts​+2kqhc​​.
(1)
The basal excess temperature is qhc​/k, twice the mean excess. The formula requires a thickness assumption and a conductive interpretation of the measured flux. Hydrothermal advection, sedimentary thermal effects, internal production and nonlinear conductivity can invalidate a linear extrapolation.

Planetary mantle

Words: 143 Articles: 4
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The planetary mantle is the predominantly silicate rock region beneath a rocky planet's crust. On geological timescales, solid rock can undergo material creep and support mantle convection without wholesale melting.

Secular cooling (dT/dt<0)

Words: 55
Planetary mantle OurBigBook.com
A long-term decline in mean interior temperature, distinct from a short transient, a local cold anomaly or a change in the pressure used for a potential temperature. In a mantle thermal budget, cooling requires heat loss to exceed internal generation plus heat entering from below. The rate depends on both the heat sources and the efficiency of transport.

Mantle transition zone

Words: 20
Planetary mantle OurBigBook.com
The region of the terrestrial mantle between major seismic discontinuities near 410 and 660 km depth, associated with mineral phase transformations.

Mantle xenolith

Words: 11
Planetary mantle OurBigBook.com
A fragment of mantle rock transported within magma to a shallower environment.

Asthenosphere

Words: 33
Planetary mantle OurBigBook.com
The asthenosphere is a relatively weak region of the upper mantle below the mechanically strong lithosphere. A seismic low-velocity zone often occurs in this region, particularly beneath oceanic lithosphere, but mechanical weakness and seismic speed are distinct properties.

Planetary crust

Words: 214 Articles: 11
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The planetary crust is the outer compositional rock layer of a differentiated rocky planet. Its thickness need not equal either the lithosphere's thermal thickness or its effective elastic thickness.

Crustal thickness (hc​)

Words: 37
Planetary crust OurBigBook.com
The distance from a body's surface to its crust-mantle boundary, under a stated geometric convention. It differs from lithosphere thickness and effective elastic thickness. Converting a vertical column thickness to a layer thickness normal to a dipping interface requires its geometry.

Mafic crust

Words: 9
Planetary crust OurBigBook.com
Crust dominated by mafic rocks, commonly basalt and gabbro or their metamorphosed equivalents.

Mohorovičić discontinuity

Words: 30
Planetary crust OurBigBook.com
The seismic boundary between crust and mantle, commonly identified by a marked increase in elastic wave speeds. It is a compositional boundary and need not coincide with the base of the lithosphere.

Continental crust

Words: 75 Articles: 4
Planetary crust OurBigBook.com
The compositionally diverse, commonly thicker and more felsic crust of continental regions.

Crustal shortening

Words: 12
Continental crust OurBigBook.com
Horizontal contraction of continental crust, commonly accommodated by folding and thrust faults and contributing to tectonic thickening.

Craton

Words: 20
Continental crust OurBigBook.com
A long-lived stable part of a continent, commonly with a thick, depleted lithospheric mantle keel; that keel is distinct from the continental crust.

Tectonic thickening

Words: 12
Continental crust OurBigBook.com
Increase in crust or lithosphere thickness through tectonic deformation, including crustal shortening and stacking by thrust faults.

Sedimentary cover

Words: 20
Continental crust OurBigBook.com
A near-surface layer of sedimentary rocks over crystalline basement; its thickness can be zero and is not a fixed fraction of continental crust.

Oceanic crust

Words: 31 Articles: 1
Planetary crust OurBigBook.com
The principally mafic compositional outer layer of an oceanic plate; it is only part of the thicker oceanic lithosphere.

Sheeted dike complex

Words: 13
Oceanic crust OurBigBook.com
An assemblage of many intrusive dikes, representing conduits feeding lavas at a spreading ridge.

Basaltic crust

Words: 7
Planetary crust OurBigBook.com
Crust dominated by basalt and compositionally related intrusive rocks.

Geodesy

Words: 94 Articles: 3
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Measurement and modeling of a planet’s shape, gravity field, orientation and deformation. Space geodesy can constrain both rigid plate motion and time-dependent solid-Earth loading response.

Gravimeter

Words: 21
Geodesy OurBigBook.com
An instrument measuring gravitational acceleration or its change. Drift, tide, platform motion and reference-height corrections are needed to interpret small gravity anomalies.

Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory

Words: 17
Geodesy OurBigBook.com
The Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory mission, which mapped the Moon's gravity using measurements between two orbiting spacecraft.

GNSS

Words: 33
Geodesy OurBigBook.com
Global navigation satellite systems can measure station position time series in a stated terrestrial reference frame. Vertical and horizontal secular or transient motions require treatment of station offsets, atmospheric delays, loading and reference-frame uncertainty.

Radial density inversion of the Earth

Words: 58 Articles: 1
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Infer a spherically averaged density profile using seismic travel times, normal-mode frequencies, mass, moment of inertia, hydrostatic structure and material constraints. Seismic speeds alone measure elastic-modulus-to-density ratios, so they do not uniquely supply density.

Preliminary Reference Earth Model

Words: 28
Radial density inversion of the Earth OurBigBook.com
A one-dimensional reference model combining elastic wave speeds, density and attenuation, developed by Adam M. Dziewonski and Don L. Anderson. It incorporates joint seismic and global integral constraints rather than treating density as a direct travel-time measurement.

Geoid

Words: 31
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
An equipotential surface of Earth gravity, including the centrifugal potential, used as an idealized sea-level reference. geoid height responds to long-wavelength density anomalies and boundary deformation; local gravity and geoid height are related but distinct observables.

Gravity anomaly

Words: 462 Articles: 13
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
A difference between observed gravity and a specified reference field after stated reductions. Free-air, Bouguer and isostatic anomalies remove different modeled effects; they are not interchangeable raw measurements.

Geophysical density contrast (Δρ=ρbody​−ρreference​)

Words: 33
Gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
The absolute density difference between a subsurface body and the material it replaces, commonly in kgm−3. It is the source term in local gravity inversion, unlike the dimensionless relative density contrast used in cosmology.

Eötvös correction

Words: 38
Gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
The correction to moving-platform gravity for the change in apparent vertical acceleration caused by motion over the rotating Earth. Eastward motion generally lowers apparent gravity and requires a positive correction; latitude and platform speed enter the full expression.

Mascon

Words: 15
Gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
A regional planetary mass concentration producing a gravity anomaly; lunar examples are associated with large impact basins.

Gravity-topography admittance (Z(k))

Words: 172 Articles: 4
Gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
A spectral transfer estimate Z(k)=⟨gk​hk∗​⟩/⟨∣hk​∣2⟩. Its wavelength dependence constrains compensation, density structure and support, but one transfer curve does not uniquely determine them.

Gravity and topography near Hawaii

Words: 43 Articles: 1
Gravity-topography admittance OurBigBook.com
The narrow volcanic ridge loads the lithosphere and generates a regional flexural response, while the broad swell involves deeper support. The observed positive ridge anomaly, negative flanks, outer positive belt, and long-wavelength positive swell anomaly probe distinct spatial scales.[ref]
Hawaiian swell
Gravity and topography near Hawaii OurBigBook.com

Gravity-topography coherence

Words: 44
Gravity-topography admittance OurBigBook.com
For cross-spectrum Sgh​ and autospectra Sgg​,Shh​, squared coherence is ∣Sgh​∣2/(Sgg​Shh​). It measures the fraction of spectral association between gravity and topography. Low coherence can signal uncorrelated internal loading, noise or shortcomings of a simple surface-load model; interpreting it as elastic thickness requires a loading model.

Flexural gravity admittance (Z(k)=2πGρc​[1−e−kt/(1+ℓf4​k4)])

Words: 61
Gravity-topography admittance OurBigBook.com
For a surface load above a uniform-density crust over a denser substrate, a simple lithospheric flexure model gives the indicated gravity-topography admittance, with ℓf4​=D/[g(ρm​−ρc​)]. The surface mass contributes positive gravity; downward displacement of the density interface contributes a compensating negative signal attenuated by e−kt. Hence Z→0 at long wavelength and Z→2πGρc​ at short wavelength. Here t is the interface depth, not automatically the effective elastic thickness.

Bouguer gravity anomaly

Words: 105 Articles: 2
Gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
A gravity anomaly after removing an approximate topographic mass contribution, often an infinite slab 2πGρh, in addition to free-air reduction. Terrain and spherical-curvature corrections refine the slab model.

Bouguer slab (Δg=2πGΔρh)

Words: 47
Bouguer gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
An ideal laterally infinite horizontal slab, whose vertical gravity anomaly is proportional to its thickness h and geophysical density contrast Δρ with replaced material. A negative geophysical density contrast gives a negative anomaly in a downward-positive convention. The slab's field above it does not specify burial depth; applying it to finite bodies is an approximation.

Terrain correction

Words: 30
Bouguer gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
A correction for the difference between real surrounding relief and the assumed simple topographic slab. Its computation needs terrain geometry and an assumed density, and can matter in rough surface topography.

Free-air gravity anomaly

Words: 72 Articles: 1
Gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
gravity reduced to a reference elevation while retaining the gravitational contribution of the intervening topographic mass. The local elevation correction is approximately 2gh/R for a spherical reference, with sign chosen to undo the measured decrease with height.

Free-air correction

Words: 35
Free-air gravity anomaly OurBigBook.com
The adjustment for measurement elevation without adding or removing the attraction of intervening terrain. Near sea level a station h metres above a datum receives an approximate +0.3086h mGal correction when reduced to that datum.

Isostasy

Words: 542 Articles: 9
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Approximate gravitational compensation of loads by subsurface mass redistribution. Airy and Pratt models use local column balances; flexural support spreads the load laterally. Real surface topography can also be maintained by dynamic stresses.

Thermal buoyancy support of topography (ΔH≃(ρs​/ρref​)αΔTL)

Words: 154
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
Suppose a compensated vertical column contains thickness L of material warmed by ΔT. For a small anomaly, the volumetric thermal expansion coefficient gives δρ≃−ρs​αΔT. Its column mass change is δM≃−ρs​αΔTL. Define ρref​ΔH to be the additional column mass associated with the permitted uplift and interface motion in the chosen isostasy model. The mass balance ρref​ΔH+δM=0 proves the displayed scaling.
The model must specify ρref​: translating an upper column of fixed internal thickness above mantle compensation gives a mantle-density scale, while fixing an internal interface and changing only surface-layer thickness gives that surface layer's density scale. If their ratio is near one, L=7 km, ΔT=350 K and α=10−5K−1 imply only about 25 m of relief. Extending this to a whole lithosphere requires its depth-dependent temperature anomaly, not only the mean temperature anomaly of the crust. Dynamic topography and flexural stresses lie outside a simple local-column calculation.

Local isostatic response to an added surface layer (w=(ρb​−ρf​)H/(ρm​−ρf​))

Words: 145
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
Let a deposited layer have thickness H and density ρb​, replacing a fluid of density ρf​, while the original crust translates downward by w above mantle of density ρm​. Assume all deposited material stays in the same fluid environment, unchanged pre-existing layer thicknesses, an external material source, and complete local isostatic adjustment without bending resistance.
At a fixed compensation depth, added column mass is (ρb​−ρf​)H per unit area, whereas depression replaces a column contrast (ρm​−ρf​)w. Equal hydrostatic pressure therefore requires
(ρb​−ρf​)gH=(ρm​−ρf​)gw.
(2)
It follows that
w=ρm​−ρf​ρb​−ρf​​H,Δz=H−w=ρm​−ρf​ρm​−ρb​​H.
(3)
The pre-existing ground subsides by w, while the top of the new layer rises by Δz if ρb​<ρm​. For a subaerial deposit, air density is negligible. For a fully submerged deposit, use seawater density. A deposit that crosses the fluid surface requires separate treatment of its submerged and emerged portions. Specifying only volume V leaves the answer dependent on loaded area through H=V/A.

Volcanic loading

Words: 44
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
Addition of erupted or intruded rock as a gravitational load on a planetary surface or interior. Deposited thickness, density, geometry and emplacement history control isostatic adjustment and lithospheric flexure. Thermal and compositional changes in the source can supply additional effects distinct from the weight of the deposited material.

Compensation depth (zc​)

Words: 30
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
A common reference depth at which lateral pressure differences are assumed relaxed in an isostatic model. It must lie below relevant lateral density anomalies; it need not be a sharp material interface.

Sediment loading

Words: 13
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
The addition of sediments as a mechanical load, contributing to subsidence through isostasy and lithospheric flexure.

Isostatic adjustment

Words: 16
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
Deformation and redistribution of material tending to restore gravitational support after a load or density distribution changes.

Isostatic ridge elevation in a plate model (h=ρm​αΔTa/[2(ρm​−ρw​)])

Words: 49
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
A cold linear plate profile has excess column mass ρm​αΔTa/2 relative to hot mantle. Equal hydrostatic pressure below the plates is restored by replacing part of the rock column with water. The displayed elevation follows to first order in thermal expansion; its denominator is the rock-minus-water density difference, not the rock density alone.

Pratt isostasy

Words: 31
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
A local compensation model in which columns of different density reach a common compensation depth. Higher surface topography is associated with a less dense column; density variation replaces the variable-root mechanism of an Airy model.

Airy isostasy (b=ρc​h/(ρm​−ρc​))

Words: 30
Isostasy OurBigBook.com
A local compensation model with approximately fixed crustal density and variable crustal thickness. A height h is supported by a crustal root b=ρc​h/(ρm​−ρc​) in a simple constant-density, air-loaded column model.

Seismology

Words: 2k Articles: 62
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Seismology studies elastic waves in a planet and uses their propagation to infer its interior and the sources of ground motion.

Seismic network

Words: 50
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A coordinated collection of recording stations with known positions and time bases. Distributed source–receiver paths constrain earthquake locations and internal wave speeds more effectively than one station. Geometry, noise, synchronization and instrument response determine which structures can be resolved; adding stations without crossing ray paths need not remove an inversion trade-off.

Receiver function

Words: 44
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A processed record that isolates relative arrival times and amplitudes of converted and reverberated seismic waves by reducing the common source and propagation response. P-to-S conversion and S-to-P conversion at contrasts in seismic velocity can constrain interface depths and sharpness. Interpretation requires a velocity model and checks for crustal multiples, dipping interfaces and seismic anisotropy.

Seismic wave

Words: 29
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A propagating disturbance in or along the solid Earth, including body P waves, body S waves and surface modes. A water layer supports compressional acoustic motion but not a bulk shear restoring force.

Seismic source

Words: 363 Articles: 8
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A natural or artificial generator of seismic waves. For an active survey its bandwidth, pulse duration, directivity and energy influence penetration, resolution and acquisition design.

Vibroseis

Words: 132 Articles: 1
Seismic source OurBigBook.com
A controlled vibratory seismic source that transmits a known frequency sweep through a coupled ground contact. Repeated sweeps can improve useful signal strength, and Vibroseis correlation compresses the long source signal into a shorter wavelet. Access, ground coupling, finite source force, bandwidth and nonlinear harmonics affect the resulting survey data.
Vibroseis correlation
Words: 87
Vibroseis OurBigBook.com
Let a linear Earth response h be recorded using a known source sweep s, giving d=s∗h+n. Cross-correlating the record with the sweep yields
c(τ)=∫d(t)s(t−τ)dt=(h∗Rss​)(τ)+Rns​(τ).
(4)
Thus a compact sweep autocorrelation Rss​ produces pulse-compressed arrival wavelets, while unrelated noise has a smaller coherent response. The Fourier transform of the result is H(ω)∣S(ω)∣2+N(ω)S(ω)​. Correlation is a matched-filter operation, not an exact inversion of missing source frequencies. Spectral shaping or stabilized deconvolution can further adjust the wavelet within the measured bandwidth.[ref]

Explosive seismic source

Words: 41
Seismic source OurBigBook.com
A seismic source producing an impulsive disturbance by a professionally managed subsurface explosion. Its applications include surveys needing strong, broad-band energy, but source coupling, repeatability, ground disturbance, site access and specialist operational requirements influence suitability. Vibroseis instead distributes controlled energy over a known frequency sweep.

Marine air-gun array

Words: 42
Seismic source OurBigBook.com
An array of compressed-air sources fired in water to generate repeatable broadband pressure pulses for a seismic reflection survey. Source tuning reduces coherent bubble oscillations but does not eliminate seismic source ghosts. Its energy and low-frequency content can provide greater penetration than small high-frequency boomer seismic sources or sparker seismic sources.

Seismic source ghost

Words: 27
Seismic source OurBigBook.com
A delayed, usually polarity-reversed copy of source radiation reflected at the water free surface. Interference with the direct wave shapes the usable spectrum; source depth controls the delay.

Sparker seismic source

Words: 36
Seismic source OurBigBook.com
A marine acoustic source using a rapid underwater electrical discharge and its expanding bubble to generate a pulse. Its energy and spectrum can be chosen to investigate shallow sub-bottom structure; bubble behaviour and seismic wavelet shape affect resolution.

Boomer seismic source

Words: 33
Seismic source OurBigBook.com
An impulsive marine acoustic source in which an electrically driven plate displaces water. The emitted broadband pulse is useful for shallow seismic reflection profiling, with effective penetration and resolution depending on source energy and substrate.

Chirp sub-bottom profiler

Words: 28
Seismic source OurBigBook.com
A shallow marine acoustic profiling system transmitting a swept-frequency pulse and using matched processing to resolve interfaces below the seabed. Fine vertical seismic resolution must be balanced against penetration and seismic attenuation.

Seismic refraction survey

Words: 31
Seismology OurBigBook.com
An acquisition and interpretation method using seismic travel times, commonly first arrivals, to constrain a velocity model. Seismic head waves can constrain faster layers, but missing velocity contrasts, hidden thin layers and low-velocity layers limit simple interpretations.

Apollo lunar seismology

Seismology OurBigBook.com
Seismic observations made by instruments emplaced during the Apollo missions, used to study moonquakes and the lunar interior.

Moonquake

Apollo lunar seismology OurBigBook.com
A seismic event originating within the Moon. Its arrival times and waveforms constrain lunar structure when recorded by a suitable seismic network. Lunar impacts are another useful seismic source but have a different origin; their known locations can help calibrate an otherwise sparse network.

Words: 50 Articles: 1
Seismology OurBigBook.com
The propagation speed of a seismic disturbance, depending on elastic properties, density, composition, temperature and microstructure.

Seismic velocity OurBigBook.com
The propagation speed of a shear elastic wave. In an ideal isotropic elastic medium it is Vs​=μ/ρ​, where μ is shear modulus and ρ mass density. Seismic anisotropy, frequency-dependent relaxation and melt can complicate the inference from an observed shear-wave velocity to temperature or composition.

Compressional-to-shear wave speed ratio (Vp​/Vs​)

Seismology OurBigBook.com
The ratio of compressional to shear elastic wave speeds. Composition, cracks, temperature and fluid saturation all affect it.

Seismicity

Seismology OurBigBook.com
The spatial and temporal occurrence of earthquakes, including their depth and magnitude distributions.

Wadati-Benioff zone

Seismicity OurBigBook.com
An inclined distribution of earthquake sources associated with a descending slab. Shallow interface earthquakes and deeper intraslab earthquakes need not share the same failure mechanism. The pattern helps trace subduction, subject to the limits of source location and the distribution of seismically active material. Named for Kiyoo Wadati and Hugo Benioff.

Words: 25
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A localized seismic waveform used to describe a source or reflected pulse. Its phase and sign determine how an impedance-driven seismic reflection polarity appears in a recorded trace.

Velocity model

Words: 26
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A description of seismic wave speed as a function of position and, if needed, direction. It converts travel times into geometric constraints and is distinct from a direct depth measurement.

Seismic reflection

Seismology OurBigBook.com
The return of an elastic wave from a contrast in material properties. At normal incidence in an isotropic medium, the conventional stress-amplitude reflection coefficient is (Z2​−Z1​)/(Z2​+Z1​) for the relevant P wave or shear-wave impedance.

Words: 67
Seismic reflection OurBigBook.com
The ratio of reflected to incident wave amplitude under a stated physical-variable and polarity convention. For normal incidence between isotropic layers with impedances Za​,Zb​, the stress-amplitude convention gives Rσ​=(Zb​−Za​)/(Za​+Zb​), while particle velocity gives Rv​=−Rσ​. The reflected energy fraction is Rσ2​ for a single lossless propagating mode. A receiver trace requires the relevant seismic wavelet, travel times and transmission factors as well as this local coefficient.

Words: 22
Seismic reflection OurBigBook.com
The inclination of a reflecting interface to horizontal. It influences seismic travel times, offset sampling and seismic migration; a reflector is not necessarily a fault plane.

Words: 25
Seismic reflection OurBigBook.com
The sign of a reflected seismic seismic wavelet relative to an incident or reference wave under a stated recording convention. A negative normal-incidence stress-amplitude reflection coefficient reverses that polarity.

A controlled-source survey recording reflected elastic waves to infer subsurface interfaces and their properties. Travel times constrain geometry through a velocity model; amplitudes also depend on source, propagation and impedance contrasts.

Seismic reflection survey OurBigBook.com
The number of source–receiver traces contributing to a midpoint bin or image location under a stated acquisition and processing scheme. Greater useful fold can improve the signal-to-noise ratio, but does not compensate for missing spatial bandwidth or an incorrect velocity model.

Words: 35
Seismic reflection survey OurBigBook.com
Processing that moves recorded reflection energy to its inferred subsurface positions using a velocity model. It corrects apparent positions of dipping reflectors and collapses suitable diffraction events; insufficient spatial sampling and incorrect velocities impair the result.

Seismic reflection survey OurBigBook.com
The ability to distinguish vertically adjacent reflectors. A quarter-wavelength thickness is a useful wavelet-tuning scale, rather than a universal exact limit; bandwidth, seismic wavelet shape and noise also matter.

Words: 20
Seismic reflection survey OurBigBook.com
Adjustment for the change in reflected travel time with source–receiver separation. A horizontal-reflector approximation gives t(x)2=t02​+x2/VNMO2​ under appropriate assumptions; a velocity model is required.

Words: 42 Articles: 1
Seismology OurBigBook.com
Reduction of seismic amplitude through intrinsic energy dissipation and scattering, distinguished from geometrical spreading.

Geometrical spreading

Words: 28
Seismic attenuation OurBigBook.com
Change in wave amplitude as the same propagating energy is distributed across changing wavefront area. It is distinct from intrinsic material absorption even though both can reduce observed amplitude with distance.

Toroidal normal mode of the Earth

Words: 50
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A toroidal normal mode of the Earth is a free oscillation with tangential, divergence-free displacement. It is the spherical counterpart of the transverse shear motion in a Love wave. A bounded spherical Earth has discrete angular orders and eigenfrequencies, so the arbitrarily low-frequency continuum of a flat infinite layer is not a literal statement about global nonrigid oscillations.

Seismic phase

Words: 34
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A seismic phase labels a propagation type and path, such as direct P, direct S, a reflection or a converted wave. Misidentifying the phase assigns the wrong travel-time function even if its arrival is picked precisely.

Low-velocity zone

Words: 85 Articles: 1
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A low-velocity zone has a wave-speed decrease with depth over some interval. Surface rays do not turn within its negative-gradient interior; rays penetrating it can return only after encountering sufficient speed recovery below. This can produce shadow ranges, multiple travel-time branches and poor turning-depth coverage. A wave-specific low-velocity zone is not identical to a mechanical layer boundary.

Seismic shadow range from a low-velocity zone

Words: 33
Low-velocity zone OurBigBook.com
A seismic shadow range is an interval of receiver distances missing a specified family of geometrical rays. A velocity decrease can separate shallow-turning and deep-turning arrivals; diffraction or other wave families can still deliver energy there.

Earthquake location by arrival times (ti​=t0​+Ti​(x))

Words: 336 Articles: 6
Seismology OurBigBook.com
Arrival-time location estimates a hypocenter and origin time by comparing picked phase arrivals with predicted travel times. Linearization gives residual changes δti​=δt0​+∇Ti​⋅δx. Poorly distinct derivative columns cause tradeoffs, while incorrect wave speeds or phase labels cause systematic bias even with many stations.

Earthquake depth–origin-time trade-off

Words: 55
Earthquake location by arrival times OurBigBook.com
For surface stations at similar distances, the travel-time derivatives with respect to depth can be small or nearly equal. Their arrival-time shifts are then difficult to distinguish from a common change in earthquake origin time. A deeper source can be paired with an earlier origin. Nearby stations, broad distance coverage, and depth-sensitive phases help separate the two parameters.

Origin-time and speed-ratio regression (tA​=t0​+Δt/(r−1))

Words: 55
Earthquake location by arrival times OurBigBook.com
If r=vA​/vB​ and both phases share path length, arrival time of A is affine in the interphase delay. With unbiased independent clock errors, the intercept estimates earthquake origin time and slope estimates 1/(r−1). A common clock bias is indistinguishable from an origin-time shift; unrestricted station offsets also destroy speed-ratio identifiability. A statistical regression must state its clock-error assumptions.

Earthquake location from interphase delays (Δt=K(x−x0​)2+z02​​)

Words: 108 Articles: 1
Earthquake location by arrival times OurBigBook.com
In a homogeneous medium, two phases along the same geometric path have delay Δt=KR, where K=1/vB​−1/vA​. The squared delay is a quadratic in station position. Its vertex locates the epicentre, while the ratio of intercept to quadratic coefficient gives squared depth. These spatial parameters do not depend on a particular assigned speed ratio if both speeds are inferred from the same data. Local clock offsets cancel, although uncertainties in the velocity model do not.
S–P time (Δt=tS​−tP​)
Words: 31
Earthquake location from interphase delays OurBigBook.com
The delay between corresponding S wave and P wave arrivals. For a common uniform path of length r, Δt=r(1/Vs​−1/Vp​), cancelling earthquake origin time. Matched phase identification and an appropriate velocity model are needed to infer distance.

Earthquake origin time (t0​)

Words: 31
Earthquake location by arrival times OurBigBook.com
An earthquake origin time is the estimated onset time of rupture. Predicted arrivals add this time to a propagation travel time; an uncertain origin time therefore couples to uncertain source depth in some station geometries.

Double-difference earthquake relocation

Words: 46
Earthquake location by arrival times OurBigBook.com
Differences between arrival times of nearby earthquakes at a common station largely cancel common propagation errors. Comparing observed and predicted differences constrains relative source separation and origin-time differences. Closely similar waveforms permit precise differential picks by cross-correlation. Absolute position still needs an accurate model or external anchor.

Seismic anisotropy

Words: 25
Seismology OurBigBook.com
Seismic anisotropy is direction dependence of elastic-wave propagation. Aligned crystals or layering can produce it; using it to infer deformation requires a model connecting fabric to flow.

Seismic ray theory

Words: 252 Articles: 6
Seismology OurBigBook.com
Seismic ray theory approximates high-frequency propagation through smoothly varying media. The travel-time field satisfies the eikonal equation, and its characteristics are paths of stationary travel time according to Fermat's principle. Diffraction and caustics require refinements beyond a simple geometrical-ray approximation.

Seismic travel time (t=∫ray​ds/V)

Words: 25
Seismic ray theory OurBigBook.com
The time for a specified seismic phase to propagate along its ray. Arrival time additionally includes earthquake origin time; those quantities must not be interchanged on an absolute-clock seismogram.

Words: 61 Articles: 1
Seismic ray theory OurBigBook.com
A ray family can fold in the mapping from ray parameter or turning depth to surface range, so that three rays arrive at the same range with different travel times. A sufficiently strong, thin high-positive-gradient zone can produce this effect. The first-arrival curve is the lower envelope of the branches; other branches represent later arrivals. Gradient contrast and thickness determine whether folds exist.
Seismic travel-time fold caustic
Seismic travel-time triplication OurBigBook.com

Words: 44
Seismic ray theory OurBigBook.com
For v(z)=vs​+βz with β>0, a surface-to-surface diving ray is circular. Its turning speed is vt​=1/p, and its range and time are X=2vt2​−vs2​​/β and T=2arcosh(vt​/vs​)/β. Differentiation gives dT/dX=p, the seismic ray parameter. In the limit β→0 at fixed range, T→X/vs​.

Words: 87 Articles: 1
Seismic ray theory OurBigBook.com
In horizontally layered isotropic media, horizontal slowness is conserved along a ray. The incidence angle i is measured from vertical. A smooth turning depth satisfies pv=1. The range and travel time are x=2∫pvdz/1−p2v2​ and T=2∫dz/[v1−p2v2​] for a symmetric surface-to-surface turning ray.

Words: 45
Seismic ray parameter in horizontal layering OurBigBook.com
A ray's intercept time subtracts its tangent travel-time contribution at the receiver range. For a smooth branch, dT/dx=p implies dτ/dp=−x. Thus an intercept-time curve encodes range as its negative slope. Separate turning branches around a low-velocity zone must be retained rather than joined by fictitious rays.

Seismic surface-wave dispersion

Words: 100 Articles: 1
Seismology OurBigBook.com
Seismic surface-wave dispersion is the frequency dependence of Rayleigh wave or Love wave propagation caused by depth-dependent elastic properties, mode structure and possibly intrinsic anelasticity. Phase velocity is ω/k; group velocity is dω/dk. Different periods and branches have different depth sensitivities, enabling surface-wave tomography.

Spherical surface-wave evanescence threshold (c<β(r)RE​/r)

Words: 68
Seismic surface-wave dispersion OurBigBook.com
For surface phase speed c on a spherical Earth, the conserved angular ray parameter is p=RE​/c. The local horizontal slowness at radius r is p/r, giving squared radial shear wavenumber qr2​=ω2[β(r)−2−p2/r2] in ray theory. The displayed inequality makes it negative. A jump in shear speed can turn a propagating wave above the interface into an evanescent wave below it. This is a local condition, not proof of evanescence at every greater depth.

Seismogram

Words: 23
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A seismogram records ground motion through an instrument response. Comparing it with a synthetic seismogram requires consistent component orientation, sampling, timing, filtering and instrument calibration.

Layer reverberation

Words: 57 Articles: 1
Seismology OurBigBook.com
Repeated reflection and conversion between a layer surface and its lower interface produces additional delayed phases. Their travel times and amplitude depend on layer thickness, wave speeds, impedance contrasts, attenuation and source spectrum.

Seismic multiple

Words: 25
Layer reverberation OurBigBook.com
A seismic phase reflected more than once before recording. Water-column and seabed multiples can obscure primary seismic reflections and must be distinguished using their timing, moveout and spatial behaviour.

Adams-Williamson equation (ρ′=−ρg/Φ)

Words: 29
Seismology OurBigBook.com
In a chemically homogeneous adiabatic spherical region, dρ/dr=−ρg/Φ, coupled to dm/dr=4πr2ρ and g=Gm/r2. Seismic velocities supply Φ; density normalization and jumps require further data and assumptions.

Seismic parameter (Φ)

Words: 22
Seismology OurBigBook.com
The adiabatic bulk modulus divided by density, Φ=KS​/ρ=α2−4β2/3 for an isotropic solid. It has units of squared speed and is a key input to the Adams-Williamson density relation.

Seismometer

Words: 94 Articles: 2
Seismology OurBigBook.com
A seismometer compares ground motion with the motion of an inertial test mass. A mechanical seismograph records their relative displacement. Its frequency response depends on the suspension and on which relative or absolute velocity enters the damping law.

Geophone

Words: 43
Seismometer OurBigBook.com
A sensor of ground motion, commonly giving an electrical response proportional to particle velocity over a specified frequency band. Three-component geophones record different motion directions and can help distinguish P- and S-wave responses. Ground coupling and orientation are essential for interpreting amplitudes and seismic reflection polarity.

Hydrophone

Words: 17
Seismometer OurBigBook.com
An underwater acoustic pressure sensor. A hydrophone streamer records fluid P waves; observing ground S waves directly instead requires coupled solid-motion sensors.

Silicate weathering

Words: 45
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Chemical alteration of silicate minerals by water and dissolved carbon dioxide. Coupled to transport and subsequent carbonate burial, this provides a long-term geological sink for added carbon. Its response is much slower than atmospheric mixing or upper-ocean exchange; a rapid pulse can persist while this adjustment proceeds.

Palaeomagnetism

Words: 270 Articles: 6
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Study of ancient magnetic fields recorded in rocks. Correlation to geomagnetic polarity chronology can constrain the age of archaeological and fossil-bearing strata.

Thermoremanent magnetization

Words: 20
Palaeomagnetism OurBigBook.com
magnetization retained as magnetic minerals cool through blocking temperatures in an ambient field. Subsequent alteration, reheating and remagnetization can change the record.

Magnetic anomaly

Words: 228 Articles: 4
Palaeomagnetism OurBigBook.com
A measured magnetic field component or magnitude after subtraction of a reference field. Source geometry, magnetization direction and observation height affect its sign and amplitude; an anomaly is not a direct map of rock polarity.

Magnetic topographic effect

Words: 67
Magnetic anomaly OurBigBook.com
A magnetic signal caused by the shape and distribution of magnetized terrain. Excavating a crater removes magnetic host rock, while its rim and remaining slopes redistribute magnetic masses. Unlike a gravity slab reduction, the effect depends on the vector magnetization, including remanence, so it has no universal density-only correction. Modelling the host and relief is necessary before attributing a crater anomaly to magnetic material in its infill.

Magnetization contrast (ΔM)

Words: 59
Magnetic anomaly OurBigBook.com
The difference ΔM=Mtarget​−Mreference​ between a target region and the reference material it replaces. A weakly magnetic crater infill inside magnetic basalt can have a negative induced contrast, even though both materials have positive magnetic susceptibility. The sign and direction of this contrast, including remanent magnetization, determine a total-field magnetic anomaly together with geometry and the ambient field. Geophysical density contrast does not determine magnetic contrast.

Total-field magnetic anomaly (ΔT)

Words: 34
Magnetic anomaly OurBigBook.com
The difference ΔT=∣B0​+b∣−∣B0​∣ between measured scalar field strength and a specified background. For ∣b∣≪∣B0​∣, it is approximately B0​⋅b, not an arbitrary fixed Cartesian component.

Marine magnetic stripe

Words: 36
Magnetic anomaly OurBigBook.com
A lineated pattern associated with differently magnetized crust formed at a spreading ridge during changes of field polarity. The age-distance relation is set by spreading, while the measured anomaly is a spatially filtered field of the magnetized material.

A region of upward air motion. In a thunderstorm, an updraft can support and transport precipitation particles and supply the liquid-water environment in which hail grows.

Meteorology OurBigBook.com
Ice precipitation grown within thunderstorms, chiefly by collection and freezing of supercooled liquid droplets. A strong updraft can retain stones in a growth region; changing growth conditions can create clear and opaque layers without requiring one complete up-and-down trip per layer.[ref]

Meteorology OurBigBook.com

Frost OurBigBook.com
The temperature at which the given water-vapour partial pressure equals saturation vapour pressure over ice. It is defined relative to ice, whereas the usual dew point uses equilibrium with liquid water.

Frozen dew

Frost OurBigBook.com

Hoar frost

Frost OurBigBook.com
An ice-crystal deposit formed directly from atmospheric water vapour on a sufficiently cold surface. It is distinguished from frozen dew, in which liquid water first condenses and subsequently freezes.[ref]

Waterspout

Words: 25
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
A rotating atmospheric column over water, with visible mist and sometimes surface spray. Fair-weather waterspouts and thunderstorm-associated tornadic waterspouts have distinct formation settings.[ref]

Halo (optical phenomenon)

Meteorology OurBigBook.com
An atmospheric optical feature produced by interactions with ice crystals. A common 22∘ halo comes from a 60∘ prism path in hexagonal crystals; minimum deviation concentrates rays near its inner angular boundary. This differs from the liquid-water path of a rainbow.[ref]

Anemometer

Dew point (TD​)

Words: 106 Articles: 2
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
The temperature at which an air parcel with a specified water vapor partial pressure first becomes saturated on cooling at fixed pressure. It solves E(TD​)=ev​ with saturation pressure E. A falling dew point during ascent does not by itself imply loss of water vapor.

Dew-point scale height in dry ascent (H=Lv​Rd​/(gRv​))

Words: 35
Dew point OurBigBook.com
Fixed water vapor mole fraction gives dlnev​=dlnp. Combining hydrostatic balance with the Clausius-Clapeyron relation yields dlnTD​/dz=−(gRv​/Lv​Rd​)(TD​/T). If TD​/T≃1, then TD​(z)≃TD​(0)e−z/H. All ratios use absolute temperature; constant latent heat, fixed composition and approximate parcel–environment temperature equality are required.

Dew-point depression (T−TD​)

Words: 36
Dew point OurBigBook.com
The difference between air temperature and its dew point. For unsaturated air it is positive. Near terrestrial surface conditions, a closed ascending parcel's lifting condensation level is approximately 125mK−1 times this difference, because its temperature decreases about 8Kkm−1 faster than its dew point.

Atmospheric circulation

Words: 57 Articles: 1
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
The large-scale movement of the atmosphere, including the tropical Hadley cell and the midlatitude Ferrel cell.

Ferrel cell

Words: 44
Atmospheric circulation OurBigBook.com
Named after William Ferrel, the thermally indirect middle-latitude mean atmospheric overturning: near-surface flow is poleward and the upper return equatorward. It is maintained largely by eddy forcing and surface stress. Its Eulerian mean thermal transport can oppose the poleward eddy contribution; it is not a second thermally direct Hadley cell.

Hadley cell

Words: 43
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
A tropical atmospheric overturning circulation with rising air near the equator, poleward flow aloft, subtropical descent and an equatorward lower return. In its ideal upper branch, conservation of angular momentum gives u=Ωasin2ϕ/cosϕ for air initially at rest relative to the equatorial surface. Eddies and friction modify this idealization.

Jet stream

Words: 50
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
A comparatively narrow band of strong atmospheric flow. Tropospheric jets are associated with large horizontal temperature gradients through the thermal wind relation; strong potential vorticity gradients can guide Rossby waves. The background speed and its spatial variation control Doppler shifting and refraction of wave packets. Not every atmospheric jet has the same origin or altitude.

Teleconnection

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
Correlated atmospheric variability between geographically separated regions. Wave propagation, mean-flow changes and coupled atmosphere–ocean forcing can produce physical connections, while statistical correlation alone does not identify a unique cause. A Rossby-wave teleconnection is an important large-scale pathway rather than an exhaustive definition of all teleconnections.

Rossby-wave teleconnection

Words: 67
Teleconnection OurBigBook.com
A spatially localized forcing, such as persistent tropical heating, can excite Rossby waves that propagate wave activity into distant regions. Mean winds Doppler-shift the waves, and background potential vorticity gradients and jets guide or refract the packets. A stationary pattern can thus connect remote ridges and troughs even though the underlying wave energy propagates. Group velocity, rather than phase velocity alone, diagnoses packet propagation; damping, seasonality and eddy feedbacks affect the response.

Lifting condensation level

Words: 60
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
The level where an initially unsaturated air parcel first reaches saturation during an approximately dry adiabatic ascent. Before saturation, expansion cools the parcel while its water-vapour mixing ratio remains approximately constant. At saturation, further ascent can condense water and release latent heat; the subsequent parcel lapse rate differs from the dry rate. Mixing with surrounding air changes this ideal parcel construction.

Foehn wind

Words: 203 Articles: 2
Meteorology OurBigBook.com
A relatively warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of a mountain. Condensation and condensate removal during ascent can produce precipitation-driven foehn warming; isentropic foehn drawdown, turbulent mixing and radiative warming can also contribute. Rainfall is therefore not a necessary condition for every foehn event. The atmosphere's upstream stratification, moisture and flow over or around the mountain determine the contributing mechanisms.[ref]

Isentropic foehn drawdown

Words: 62
Foehn wind OurBigBook.com
Mountain blocking can prevent low-level upstream air from crossing the barrier while air from higher levels passes over and descends. In stable stratification that elevated source air has higher potential temperature; adiabatic descent can bring it into a lee valley warmer than the blocked low-level air. This source-air change permits a dry foehn without requiring condensation and rainout along the arriving parcel's path.

Precipitation-driven foehn warming (ΔT≃(Γd​−Γm​)(H−zc​))

Words: 76
Foehn wind OurBigBook.com
In the classical idealized parcel path, ascend dry adiabatically to condensation height zc​, continue at constant moist lapse rate Γm​ to height H>zc​, lose condensate, then descend at dry lapse rate Γd​ to the initial height. Adding the temperature changes gives the title. Complete condensate removal and an unsaturated descent are essential assumptions. A reversible dry ascent and descent with the same source air instead gives no net temperature increase at the same pressure.

Meteorology OurBigBook.com
The temperature a parcel would have after reversible adiabatic compression to a reference pressure. For a dry ideal gas, θ=T(p0​/p)R/cp​; it is conserved for dry adiabatic motion.

For a dry fixed-composition ideal gas with constant specific heats, ds=cp​dlnT−Rd​dlnp. Defining θ=T(p0​/p)Rd​/cp​ gives the displayed identity. Reversible adiabatic parcel motion conserves entropy and theta simultaneously. Irreversible entropy production or moist latent heating can change ordinary dry theta even without heat exchanged through the parcel boundary.

Condensed water falling from clouds or deposited from the atmosphere as liquid or solid particles. It can efficiently scavenge soluble gases and aerosol particles. Gas conversion into sulfate and subsequent atmospheric precipitation removal are separate stages of an atmospheric sulfur budget.

Liquid-water precipitation reaching the surface. In a catchment water balance its rate is an input measured as water depth per time; only the part not absorbed or otherwise lost becomes rainfall excess feeding overland flow.

Nucleation creates the initial ice embryo, either within liquid or with assistance from a suitable interface. Deposition, riming and ice-crystal aggregation enlarge already existing ice. Small-particle nucleation probabilities depend on thermodynamic driving, interfaces, volume and exposure time.

Weather forecasting estimates future meteorological conditions from observations and physical models. Numerical models use an approximate initial condition and equations of fluid mechanics to simulate future conditions; forecasters also compare model outputs and apply experience and research.[ref] The forecast horizon describes how far ahead a prediction remains useful at a specified accuracy; sensitive dependence on initial conditions can limit detailed predictions under deterministic evolution.

An ensemble runs multiple forecasts with perturbed initial states, model parameters or physical formulations to represent uncertainty. Its distribution can indicate probabilities and sensitivity, but finite sampling or shared model errors can make the ensemble underdispersive. Growing initial perturbations can be selected using right singular vectors of a finite-time propagator.

In a linear Gaussian update, analysis increments are K(y−Hxb​) with K=BHT(HBHT+R)−1, where B and R are prior and observation error covariance matrices. Observation noise, sparse coverage and incorrect model or covariance assumptions can all leave forecast errors.

Under standard fixed-temperature salt-contrast dynamics, the stronger positive and reversed branches are stable, while the weaker positive branch is unstable. This positive feedback permits bistability and a saddle-node bifurcation.

Albedo (α)

Words: 818 Articles: 5
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Albedo is the fraction of incident electromagnetic radiation power reflected, summed over the outgoing directions included in the measurement. For incident power Pin​>0 and reflected power Pref​,
α=Pin​Pref​​,0≤α≤1.
(5)
Thus α=0.30 means 30 percent reflected. For an opaque surface the remaining 70 percent is absorbed; for a transmitting layer, transmission must also be accounted for. Specify the incident wavelengths and illumination geometry: a visible-band surface albedo and a sunlight-weighted broadband surface albedo need not agree. NASA's definition explicitly allows a specified spectral band. [ref]
For a whole planet, broadband Bond albedo sums reflected power over all outgoing directions and all incident wavelengths, weighted by the illuminating spectrum. It is the fraction needed for a whole-planet absorbed-sunlight budget. A local surface albedo describes one surface under specified illumination; it cannot simply replace the Bond albedo of Earth, whose clouds and terrestrial atmosphere also reflect and absorb sunlight. Nor is Bond albedo the same as geometric albedo, which compares brightness in a particular viewing geometry. NASA's account of Earth's budget separates reflection by clouds, particles and the surface from absorption within the terrestrial atmosphere and at the surface. [ref]
The usefulness of albedo is that it turns optical behavior into an energy budget. Bright snow and sea ice usually absorb less sunlight than exposed water under comparable illumination, but their actual surface albedos depend on the spectrum and surface conditions. The ice-ocean albedo feedback makes that optical property part of the dynamics, while the following zero-dimensional planetary energy balance isolates the geometry and competing thermal radiation.

(6)
where α is the broadband Bond albedo. The factor four is a sphere geometry result, not an atmospheric transmission factor. Local sunlight still varies over the illuminated hemisphere and vanishes on the dark side.
Now stipulate a single spatially uniform temperature T, no atmosphere, no internal heating, and emissivity one for outgoing thermal radiation. This is a thermal blackbody model using the Stefan–Boltzmann law; the prescribed solar-band reflection is treated separately, so the body is not a perfect absorber at all wavelengths. CdtdT​=F(T),F(T)=4S​[1−α(T)]−σT4.

[ref] The uniform temperature is a model assumption: generally the surface average of T4 differs from the fourth power of the surface-average temperature.

T∗​=[4σS(1−α)​]1/4.

Fixed Bond albedoReflected average (Wm−2)Absorbed average (Wm−2)Equilibrium temperature (K)
0.30102238254.531

Doubling albedo here lowers the equilibrium temperature by 33.231K, rather than halving it: the absorbed fraction changes from 0.7 to 0.4, and thermal radiation scales as T4. These stipulated Bond albedos are whole-planet examples, not measurements of bare water and ice. The model predicts neither Earth's modern surface temperature nor its response to actual climate change; it omits the greenhouse effect, spatial heat transfer and seasons.
Each fixed-albedo equilibrium is a stable equilibrium: for T∗​>0, the derivative is F′(T∗​)=−4σT∗3​<0. A small temperature increase produces net cooling, and a small decrease produces net heating. This is the simplest expression of the stabilizing Planck feedback. Allowing albedo to fall with temperature adds a competing term, as in ice-ocean albedo feedback.

A convective chimney is a localized deeply mixed region formed when surface buoyancy loss overcomes ocean density stratification. Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Ice-ocean albedo feedback is the ocean-surface case of ice-albedo feedback: loss of bright sea ice, often covered by snow, exposes darker water, lowers surface albedo and increases absorbed sunlight. The extra stored ocean heat content can promote further melting and delay refreezing. Reversing the sequence can amplify cooling. This is a positive climate feedback, meaning that it reinforces the initial change; the word positive does not mean beneficial, and it does not guarantee runaway warming.
For unchanged downward solar irradiance S↓​ on a newly exposed opaque patch, the extra absorbed heat flux is
ΔFabs​=(αice​−αwater​)S↓​.
(9)
For illustrative local surface albedos 0.60 and 0.10, and S↓​=200Wm−2, the patch absorbs an additional 100Wm−2. This is a local sunlight calculation, not a whole-planet radiative forcing: newly exposed area, illumination, clouds and season determine its global contribution. With no incident sunlight this particular heating pathway vanishes. NASA's notes describe the contrast between reflective ice and snow and darker water. [ref]
To isolate how a positive climate feedback competes with Planck feedback, retain the assumptions of the zero-dimensional planetary energy balance and prescribe the smooth broadband Bond albedo
α(T)=0.3+1+exp[(T−240K)/(3K)]0.3​.
(10)
The exponential function makes a smooth transition from a bright cold state near 0.6 to a darker warm state near 0.3. The midpoint 240K and width 3K are chosen to illustrate the dynamics. They are not a seawater freezing law, an observed global relation, or a calibration of modern Earth. No evolving ice thickness or latent heat is represented.
An equilibrium satisfies F(T∗​)=0. For a small perturbation δT, linear stability follows from
CdtdδT​≃F′(T∗​)δT,F′(T)=−4S​α′(T)−4σT3.
(11)
Since C>0, F′<0 gives an asymptotically stable equilibrium, while F′>0 gives an unstable equilibrium. With x=(T−240K)/(3K), the derivative is
α′(T)=−3K0.3​(1+ex)2ex​<0.
(12)
Thus the optical term −Sα′/4 is destabilizing, while the thermal radiation term −4σT3 is stabilizing. Their sum, not the optical term alone, decides the linear stability.
For the same S=1360Wm−2 and Stefan-Boltzmann constant used above, the bisection method on the intervals (220,223), (238,241) and (253,255), with temperature in kelvins, gives:
Equilibrium temperature (K)Bond albedo α(T∗​)F′(T∗​) (Wm−2K−1)Behavior
221.3840.599396−2.392633Asymptotically stable cold equilibrium
240.2110.444731+5.345752Unstable equilibrium
254.3010.302530−3.445726Asymptotically stable warm equilibrium
Unrounded numerical zeros of a function have ∣F(T∗​)∣<10−10Wm−2; the table rounds them for readability. In the positive-temperature domain the sign of F alternates between heating, cooling, heating and cooling across these three equilibria. The middle equilibrium separates the basins of attraction of the two stable equilibria. For example, a starting temperature of 235K cools toward the cold state, whereas 245K warms toward the warm state: this is bistability at identical external illumination.
The same model illustrates hysteresis. Its equilibrium curve can be written as S(T)=4σT4/[1−α(T)]. The two turning points, where 4[1−α(T)]+Tα′(T)=0, are saddle-node bifurcations: approximately (T,S)=(232.637K,1567.801Wm−2) and (245.893K,1250.481Wm−2). For illumination strictly between these thresholds there are two stable equilibria and one unstable equilibrium. Under sufficiently slow increase of S, the cold branch ends at the upper threshold; under sufficiently slow decrease, the warm branch ends at the lower threshold. The ensuing warming and cooling transitions differ, so the state depends on its history. Finite sweep rates can delay the transitions; these thresholds describe this model's static equilibrium curve, not predicted tipping points for modern Earth.
The striking feature is that a smooth albedo law can produce distinct long-time states and abrupt transitions, although no discontinuity was inserted into the optical law. It is useful for understanding why positive climate feedback can amplify a response while stabilizing thermal radiation still limits it. Here 0.3<α(T)<0.6 bounds the incoming heating, whereas outgoing thermal radiation grows as T4; high enough temperatures therefore cool rather than run away indefinitely.
Historically, M. I. Budyko's 1969 paper coupled changing albedo from expanding ice cover to a latitude-dependent temperature and heat transfer calculation, showing how that coupling amplified the effect of changed sunlight. [ref] William D. Sellers's 1969 paper constructed an annual energy-budget model in 10-degree latitude belts, including planetary albedo, atmospheric infrared transmission and atmospheric and oceanic exchange. [ref] These primary papers provide historical examples of ice-sensitive energy-budget modeling; the smooth single-temperature example above is a separate illustration, not a reproduction of either paper's equations or predictions.

Each level answers different questions. A column can explain why changing an absorber changes surface temperature; it cannot locate tomorrow's storm.
Three questions should be kept distinct: what sets an average temperature, how fast does it respond to radiative forcing, and how large are its unforced fluctuations? Climate sensitivity concerns the first, heat capacity controls response times, and the Hasselmann stochastic climate model illustrates the third. A radiative-convective climate column applies a radiative-convective equilibrium model to the vertical thermal structure relevant to climate change. Radiative transfer determines heating and cooling; convective adjustment represents unresolved vertical redistribution when the chosen atmospheric lapse rate is too steep. Radiative equilibrium alone need not give a physically admissible lower-atmospheric profile.
In 1967, Syukuro Manabe and Richard T. Wetherald computed equilibrium with prescribed relative humidity, allowing atmospheric water vapor to change with temperature. Their average-cloud case warmed by 2.36K for carbon dioxide increasing from 300 to 600 parts per million, versus 1.33K with fixed absolute humidity. These are model outputs, not measured warming. The comparison isolates an important water-vapor feedback.[ref]
An original two-temperature calculation exposes the bookkeeping. Let an opaque surface absorb solar irradiance Q and emit blackbody thermal radiation σTs4​. A single isothermal atmospheric layer transmits all sunlight and absorbs a fraction ϵ of surface infrared emission, emitting ϵσTa4​ both upward and downward. This is a grey thermal-band emissivity, with 0<ϵ≤1. Let H be upward nonradiative heat flux, and let Cs​,Ca​>0 be heat capacities per unit area. Then conservation of energy gives
Cs​T˙s​=Q+ϵσTa4​−σTs4​−H,Ca​T˙a​=ϵσTs4​−2ϵσTa4​+H.
(13)
The two equations sum to
dtd​(Cs​Ts​+Ca​Ta​)=Q−L,L=(1−ϵ)σTs4​+ϵσTa4​.
(14)
Here L is outgoing longwave radiation. Both H and downward atmospheric emission cancel internally: they redistribute energy without creating it. The factor two in atmospheric emission counts two faces. Dropping the downward face would spoil the surface budget. Each right-hand term has units Wm−2; each C has units Jm−2K−1.
Choose Q=240Wm−2, H=80Wm−2 and ϵ=1. At equilibrium, L=σTa4​=240Wm−2 and σTs4​=400Wm−2, giving Ta​≃255.06K and Ts​≃289.81K. Direct substitution gives surface balance 240+240−400−80=0 and atmospheric balance 400−480+80=0. These deliberately chosen fluxes illustrate the model; they are not an observed global budget or a reconstruction of the 1967 calculation. Prescribing H illustrates heat transfer accounting but does not close a realistic convection law.
For fixed Q,H,ϵ, the positive-temperature equilibrium is locally stable. Put a=4σTs3​>0 and b=4ϵσTa3​>0. The Jacobian matrix of the temperature equations has trace −a/Cs​−2b/Ca​<0 and determinant ab(2−ϵ)/(Cs​Ca​)>0. Thus both eigenvalues have negative real part. Temperature-dependent climate feedbacks alter this test. A single grey layer also omits the optical spectrum, cloud structure and the independent thermal behavior of the troposphere and stratosphere.

Convective adjustment replaces an excessively steep vertical temperature gradient by an allowed profile while respecting the selected energy budget. For an original dry two-slab example, take fixed equal heat capacities and slab centers separated by Δz=2km. Initially T1​=300K below and T2​=280K above. Stipulate a permitted atmospheric lapse rate Γc​=6Kkm−1. The initial difference 20K exceeds the allowed 12K. Conservation of the sum of the two sensible energies requires T1′​+T2′​=580K, while the adjusted gradient requires T1′​−T2′​=12K. Hence T1′​=296K and T2′​=284K. Heat removed below equals heat added above. Simply holding the lower slab fixed and raising the upper slab to 288K would introduce external energy.
For unequal constant heat capacities C1​,C2​, the same two constraints instead give
T1′​=C1​+C2​C1​T1​+C2​T2​+C2​Γc​Δz​,T2′​=T1′​−Γc​Δz.
(15)
Apply this adjustment only when the original gradient exceeds the threshold. A moist adjustment also has to account for latent heat and changing composition; conservation of this dry sensible-energy expression alone is then insufficient.

Words: 504
Climate model OurBigBook.com
The Hasselmann stochastic climate model represents slowly responding climate variables driven by fast weather fluctuations as well as external forcing. Klaus Hasselmann's 1976 paper separates fast and slow variables, retains fluctuations lost by simple averaging, and explains why stabilizing climate feedbacks are needed to prevent indefinitely growing variability. Its general framework is broader than a single-temperature equation.[ref]
Consider an original scalar specialization for a spatially averaged temperature anomaly T, with an effective ocean mixed layer heat capacity per unit area C:
CdtdT​=F(t)−λT+η(t),C>0,λ>0.
(16)
Here F is imposed radiative forcing, λ is the net restoring coefficient after the chosen climate feedbacks, and η represents random net heat flux from unresolved weather. The anomaly energy per unit area is CT, so its tendency equals the net input. The weather term represents exchange with omitted degrees of freedom; it does not assert that an isolated ocean creates energy. F and η have units Wm−2, and λ has units Wm−2K−1.
First set η=0, start from T(0)=0, and switch to constant F0​>0. The integrating factor eλt/C gives
T(t)=λF0​​(1−e−t/τ),τ=λC​.
(17)
For C=2.0×108Jm−2K−1, λ=2.0Wm−2K−1 and F0​=4.0Wm−2, the relaxation time is 108s, about 3.17 years using 365.25 days per year. At t=τ, T=2(1−e−1)K≃1.264K, with eventual warming 2K. Doubling C doubles the response time but leaves this equilibrium unchanged. This separates thermal inertia from climate sensitivity.
Now set F=0 and idealize the weather forcing as Gaussian white noise with
Eη(t)=0,E[η(t)η(t′)]=2Dδ(t−t′),D>0.
(18)
The Dirac delta function has inverse-time units, so D has units (Wm−2)2s. The rigorous stochastic differential equation is
dT=−Cλ​Tdt+C2D​​dWt​,
(19)
where Wt​ is Brownian motion. This is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. In stationary initialization its variance and autocovariance function are
v∞​=CλD​,RT​(u)=v∞​e−∣u∣/τ.
(20)
Define the two-sided angular-frequency power spectral density by RT​(u)=(2π)−1∫−∞∞​ST​(ω)eiωudω. The Fourier transform of the exponential autocovariance function, or the squared response to a sinusoidal input, gives
ST​(ω)=λ2+C2ω22D​,ST​(0)ST​(ω)​=1+(ωτ)21​.
(21)
Thus fast fluctuations are suppressed; the climate output is red over the frequency range above the corner ∣ω∣=1/τ, with a low-frequency plateau. This is a colored noise spectrum without a periodic driver. The corner is fc​=1/(2πτ) in cycles per second, not 1/τ. The continuous white input is only an approximation on times longer than weather's correlation time.
For the same C,λ and D=108(Wm−2)2s, v∞​=0.25K2 and the stationary standard deviation is 0.50K. From fixed T(0)=0, the variance grows as v∞​(1−e−2t/τ), even when the forced expected value is predictable. Integrating ST​/(2π) over all angular frequencies returns D/(Cλ), checking the normalization independently. If λ=0 the unforced variance instead grows as 2Dt/C2; if λ<0, deviations amplify. Neither case has the stationary spectrum above.
A red spectrum alone cannot establish attribution of recent climate change: internal variability, changing forcing and measurement effects must be distinguished. This scalar model supplies a calculable baseline for variability and persistence, not a universal spectrum for all climate timescales or a full attribution analysis.

Climate model OurBigBook.com
A satellite test of greenhouse spectral change compares outgoing radiance with radiative transfer predictions. The 2001 study compared IRIS on Nimbus 4 (1970) and IMG on ADEOS (1997). Matching April–June ocean regions, masking land, screening clouds and correcting resolution and wavenumber controlled comparability. Spectral radiance became brightness temperature readouts. Regional comparisons and independent calculations tested interpretation. Carbon dioxide and methane features supported changed absorption; residual clouds, calibration and interannual variability limited background inference.[ref]
This observational comparison tests radiative transfer; it does not by itself measure equilibrium climate sensitivity or validate a complete climate model.
To understand the readout, write an instrument's spectral channel schematically as
yj​=∫Kj​(ν)I(ν,n)dν+bj​+ej​,∫Kj​(ν)dν=1.
(22)
Here I is spectral radiance in the viewing direction n, Kj​ is a normalized channel response, bj​ is calibration offset and ej​ is random error. Subtracting two channel readings isolates an atmospheric difference only after their response functions and sampling are comparable. Matching kernels reduces a false difference caused merely by observing a narrow spectral line at different resolutions; it cannot remove every calibration offset.
Outgoing longwave radiation in an energy budget also integrates radiance over upward directions and over the thermal spectrum, with the appropriate projected-angle factor. A brightness temperature converts one spectral radiance to the equivalent blackbody value through Planck's law; it is not automatically surface temperature. This explains why a spectral difference, a broadband radiative flux difference and surface warming are related observables with different units and different inferences.

For a cohesionless, optimally oriented normal fault with vertical maximum compression and horizontal minimum compression,
δ=45∘+2φ​,μf​=tanφ=tan(2δ−90∘),
(30)
where δ is fault dip and φ the internal friction angle. This is a geometric inference under the model, not a measurement of friction from dip alone.
For a compression-positive Mohr circle, put C=(σ1′​+σ3′​)/2 and R=(σ1′​−σ3′​)/2. Tangency to the cohesionless Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion τ=μf​σn′​ gives R/C=sinφ. The contact point is (σn′​,τ)=(Ccos2φ,Csinφcosφ). The physical plane-normal angle to σ1′​ is half the corresponding central angle, giving the stated dip. Equivalently the plane itself makes 45∘−φ/2 with σ1′​.
The associated stress ratio is σ1′​/σ3′​=(1+sinφ)/(1−sinφ). A reactivated nonoptimal plane, nonzero cohesion or unknown principal stress directions defeats the simple dip-only inversion.
